interest: This collection offers a granular look at SCAP’s gatekeeping apparatus as occupied Japan transitioned from strict postwar isolation toward private international commerce and experimental tourism. For historians, it illuminates both early Cold War security anxieties—such as the surveillance of Soviet-bloc travelers—and the complex diplomatic hurdles faced by stateless refugees and newly partitioned or non-represented nations navigating Allied occupation policies.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP)
overview: This file comprises extensive State Department, Army, Commerce Department, and diplomatic records from late 1947 through mid-1948 documenting the regulation of travel, residence, and trade in Allied-occupied Japan, Korea, and Okinawa. It details the administrative and logistical machinery of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) governing entry clearances, military permits, and exit-permit waivers for foreign commercial agents, missionaries, and returning residents. Key subjects include the formalization of rules for private trade under SCAP Circular No. 3 and the Guide for Commercial Entrants to Japan, diplomatic protocols requiring third-country nationals to apply via protecting powers, early plans for organized seven-day package tours, refugee and repatriation movements, and emerging Cold War surveillance protocols targeting Soviet and Soviet-satellite travelers transiting Far East Command areas.
